Anwar Nusseibeh photographed in 1967 (Boris Carmi/ Licence: WC-BY-4.0)

Lana Nusseibeh’s late grandfather was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, Middle East Eye can reveal.
The United Arab Emirates’ candidate to be the United Nations’ secretary general has said politics is “in my blood… Grandfathers on both sides were involved in politics.”
And indeed, Nusseibeh’s paternal grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician and a minister in Jordan, who'd joined the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1940s.
He was a staunch believer in democracy, lost a leg defending Jerusalem against Zionist militia in 1948 and advocated a one-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict.
The UAE, an absolute monarchy, bans the Muslim Brotherhood, an organisation promoting political Islam. Abu Dhabi has sought to attack numerous Muslim groups across the world, including in the US and Europe, by accusing them of links to the Brotherhood.
Lana Nusseibeh herself has denounced the Brotherhood as a terrorist organisation, including in a 2020 debate at the UN General Assembly.
MEE has uncovered documents that show her grandfather was a member of the Brotherhood, which had a chapter in Jerusalem in the 1940s and supported democratic participation, as the organisation’s mainstream does today.
A letter in Arabic sent to Anwar Nusseibeh on 8 June 1946 by the Brotherhood’s Jerusalem chapter reads: “The Board of the Society of the Muslim Brothers is pleased to inform you of its decision to accept you as a member of the Society.
“The Board has every hope that the Society will reap the richest fruits from your valued efforts towards its noblest aims. We ask God for success and right guidance.”

Submitted by

on

Baghdad wants to set the first stone in January with Erdogan attending, Turkish Transportation Minister Uraloglu tells MEE
An aerial photo taken in October 2022 shows the Grand Faw Port project, which is under construction in the southern Iraqi city of Basra (AFP)
Off
Turkey and Iraq have finalised a deal to fund the 12,000km Iraq Development Road and aim to sign it before the end of the year, Turkish Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told Middle East Eye.
Uraloglu, who met his counterparts and other senior officials in Baghdad on Wednesday, said the two sides had resolved all outstanding issues over financing the $16bn project. It was now only a matter of time before they signed the deal, he said.
“Iraq's government would like to set the first stone in January with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan present,” the minister told MEE.
First unveiled in May 2023 as a “dry canal”, the project would connect Iraq’s Grand Faw port in Basra to Turkey and Europe by rail and road, potentially adding energy links. It has faced several obstacles since then.
Regional officials told MEE that some of the original partners, including the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, were unable to provide funding, prompting Baghdad and Ankara to look for alternatives.
Uraloglu said the two sides had agreed on an oil-for-construction scheme developed by Ankara.
“We have a scheme where Iraq would sell 130,000 or 150,000 barrels of oil per day to Turkey and the money would be allocated to fund the project,” the minister said, adding that they prioritise the railway, which would require fibre optics throughout the route, allowing also a data link to be established from Basra to Turkey.

"American Doctor was always meant to be a decoy, a Trojan horse."
On the surface, American Doctor is a film about three American doctors who volunteered in Gaza's hospitals during Israel's war. But for director Poh Si Teng, the title was always a way in: a film to reach audiences in the West, about Palestinian health workers and the US-made bombs falling on them.
The film follows trauma surgeon Dr Feroze Sidhwa, Palestinian-American emergency physician Dr Thaer Ahmad and Dr Mark Perlmutter, from Gaza's hospitals to the halls of power in Washington.

United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is seen at a ceremony in Paris, France, on 19 July 2022 (AFP)
Off
An explosive new book by veteran journalist Matthew Cole claims Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Middle East envoy, had a deep entanglement with the governments of Saudi Arabia and particularly the UAE, during the first Trump administration.
The book's most explosive claim is that Kushner was given approximately $2bn from the Saudi and Emirati governments, including $750m held at First Abu Dhabi Bank through an Emirati charity, Watani Al Emarat Foundation, ostensibly to support civic programs in the Emirates, but in reality used for Emirati weapons purchases and covert military operations.
Kushner, who is currently acting as an envoy for Trump in Ukraine and the Middle East, has vociferously denied the claims.
But the New York Times said the allegations against Kushner should be investigated when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.
The book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East, published last month, contains dozens of other juicy nuggets about the Middle East and the wheeling and dealing that takes place in the region. It also provides a window into the culture of the UAE’s ruling Al Nahyan family.
Cole’s sources are anonymous and MEE couldn’t independently verify all the claims but has selected several highlights below.
Homosexual blackmail

Settlers smash foundations of Palestinian family's homes in West Bank
Israeli settlers smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank on Thursday, after settler attacks prevented the family from returning to them in defiance of an Israeli court order.
Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the hilltop two-storey houses on either side of a road in the village of Jaloud after midnight and spending about an hour damaging the houses. The family said it had been forced out months ago.
"This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators," said Ghiath Nasser, a lawyer representing the owners of the houses in court.
The demolition follows a surge of settler violence in which settlers have encroached on Palestinian villages, with an average of 53 settler attacks per week since the start of 2026, according to UN figures.
Reporting by Reuters
